name: Oxide Computer Company
origin_detail: Started in 2019 by Bryan Cantrill, Steve Tuck and Jess Frazelle (announced 2019-12-02) with Eclipse Ventures as lead investor, to co-design rack-scale hardware and software for on-premises cloud, crediting open firmware and the Open Compute Project as what made the company feasible. Headquartered in Emeryville, California (per its October 2026 Series D release).
openness_notes: Hardware column. Oxide publishes its firmware and software stack: Hubris (service-processor OS, MPL-2.0), the Omicron control plane (MPL-2.0) and hundreds of other public repositories (434 on GitHub as of 2026-11), plus public RFDs. Its own board designs are not published: no PCB, schematic or CAD repositories were found, and Hubris notes that Gemini bring-up documentation lives in an internal repository. Open firmware and software with closed hardware designs is level 2, unchanged since the first product shipped in 2023.

license_history.note: Year approximate: Hubris was proposed in Oxide RFD 41; the date of its public release was not verified.

risk_events: 2019-2023: about four years of development before first product; $89M raised before the Series B
2025-2026: demand exceeding supply and a large order backlog required large inventory financing (Series C $200M, Series D $445M plus debt facilities)
Hardware designs and supply chain are proprietary and single-vendor, so customers depend on Oxide's survival for hardware even though the software is open
2026: reported reaching profitability earlier in the year and scaling manufacturing capacity 20x in 12 months, with demand still exceeding supply (Series D release, 2026-10-09)
2026-11: Micron invested through Micron Ventures (amount undisclosed) as Micron memory and storage ship in Oxide's second-generation rack
robustness: Software and firmware are public under MPL-2.0, so customers could in principle maintain the stack, but the hardware is proprietary and made only by Oxide. Financially stronger in 2026: it reported paying income tax for the first time on operating profit and raised $645M in disclosed rounds in 2026 from existing investors plus Atreides Management and AMD Ventures, followed by an undisclosed Micron Ventures investment in November 2026.
physical_science_relevance: Sells on-premises cloud racks to government and national-lab customers (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory announcement, Nov 2024; Carahsoft public-sector partnership, Sep 2026); relevant to research computing that cannot use public cloud.
openness_effect_assessment: Oxide treats open firmware and software as a transparency and trust feature: its Series B post says prospective customers often examined the source code itself, and the founders credit open firmware and OCP for making the company feasible. Openness did not extend to the hardware designs, which remain the proprietary product. Funding grew from $89M before mid-2025 to about $834M by October 2026, so open firmware has not hindered fundraising.
key_takeaway: Oxide is the 'open firmware, closed boards' pattern at rack scale: everything from the service-processor OS to the control plane is MPL-2.0 on GitHub, but revenue comes from selling proprietary integrated racks. It is a US example of a long, capital-heavy hardware build-out (four years to first product) that by 2026 reported taxable profit and backlog-driven fundraising, and it builds directly on the Open Compute Project's open rack ideas.

unconfirmed.reason: No page states the $834M total. Its components were checked against Oxide's own PR Newswire releases, which are different pages from the cited blog posts. Series B: '$100 million Series B financing round led by Thomas Tull's US Innovative Technology Fund' (2025-07-30), which 'more than doubles Oxide's capital raised to date', consistent with $89M before it. Series C: '$200 million Series C led by Thomas Tull's US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT)' (2026-02-10), 'doubling total funding for the second time'. Series D: $445M (2026-10-09). The $89M raised before Series B rests on the cited Series B blog post alone.

verification_pass2.note: The Series C blog post is dated 2026-02-05, but its PR Newswire release is dated 2026-02-10. The release says USIT led the round. USIT led the Series B, so it was an existing investor, which fits Oxide's statement that the round came from existing investors. There is no Wikipedia article on Oxide. Bryan Cantrill's article says only 'He is now the co-founder and CTO of Oxide Computer company', with no year. No official page states a valuation, so latest_value stays null. Confidence stays medium because the total is a sum, not a stated figure.
